content: An evaluation of a policy implemented in Uganda to treat all children under 15 years of age revealed a 74% increase in the number of children newly initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) and an increase in ART coverage among children from 22% to 32% between 2013 and 2014. There was no observed decline in testing or ART coverage for infants, and the proportion of children receiving ART at lower-level health facilities rose from 29% to 35%. This suggests that simplifying the criteria for initiating treatment can facilitate the decentralization of ART services. Additionally, the time from eligibility to ART initiation significantly decreased, indicating that simpler initiation criteria enabled faster treatment initiation. Programmatic experience indicates that children receiving ART have better retention in care compared to those who are in care but not receiving ART. Retention rates in Uganda were comparable among children starting ART when eligible or with CD4 counts above 500 cells/mm³. However, there was a reduction in retention at six months, emphasizing the need for appropriate counseling and support for children and caregivers to maintain care engagement. Potential harms of earlier ART initiation include short-term side effects that may lead to suboptimal adherence and treatment failure, as well as the emergence of drug resistance and the need for secondand third-line regimens, which remain limited for children. Treatment failure was observed in 10% of cases in a multi-cohort analysis, with higher risks associated with longer durations on ART and older age at ART initiation. Increasing demands on the health system, drug stock-outs, and treatment discontinuation may also contribute to treatment failure and HIV drug resistance. Long-term side effects and chronic disease may increase morbidity and impact quality of life in adulthood. However, the clinical and programmatic benefits of earlier ART initiation are likely to outweigh these potential harms. Expanding ART to all children living with HIV is expected to improve equity and be well-accepted. Community consultations revealed that parents, caregivers, and healthcare providers supported earlier treatment for children due to perceived health benefits. However, psychosocial support for parents and caregivers, particularly regarding disclosure, was identified as critical for facilitating treatment initiation and improving adherence. Implementing this recommendation is considered feasible, as it represents a relatively small additional burden on current health systems. Late diagnosis remains common, with an estimated 80% or more of children identified as HIV-positive already eligible for ART under WHO 2013 recommendations. However, increasing the number of children receiving ART may place higher demands on supply chain systems and increase provider workloads. Strengthening laboratory monitoring will be necessary to assess treatment efficacy and identify treatment failure among children. National program experiences have demonstrated the feasibility of treating all children with HIV but highlight the importance of secure commodity supplies, adequate health worker training, and sustainable resources. Increased demand for HIV commodities, human resources, and infrastructure may require additional funding. Cost analyses in Zambia indicate that antiretroviral drugs are the most significant cost driver, accounting for 81% of total costs among children aged 0–14 years, followed by laboratory commodities, human resources, and co-trimoxazole. As ART is expanded to all children regardless of clinical and immune status, priority should be given to children younger than 2 years or those with WHO stage 3 or 4 disease, CD4 percentage below 25%, or CD4 counts at or below 750 cells/mm³ (if younger than 5 years) and CD4 counts at or below 350 cells/mm³ (if older than 5 years) due to their higher risk of death and rapid disease progression. Implementation approaches should leverage opportunities to deliver ART for children in maternal, newborn, and child health settings. Expanding ART services for children will require strategies to improve retention in care and support adherence. Clinical monitoring remains essential to assess the risk of treatment failure, but the lack of laboratory monitoring should not be a barrier to initiating ART. Further research is needed to understand how earlier ART affects retention, adherence, and potential HIV drug resistance among children with less advanced disease. Optimal service delivery models are also required to ensure rapid identification and ART initiation among HIV-infected infants and children, as well as strategies to provide integrated care to reduce overall child mortality. For patients with HIV-associated tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated in all TB patients living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count, as soon as possible and within the first 8 weeks of TB treatment. For those with CD4 counts less than 50 cells/mm³, ART should be started within the first two weeks of initiating TB treatment. Early ART initiation has been shown to reduce overall mortality, particularly in patients with profound immunosuppression (CD4 counts <50 cells/mm³). However, early ART initiation is associated with a higher incidence of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), which may require additional resources for diagnosis and management. Patients with TB meningitis require caution, as immediate ART is associated with more severe adverse events compared to ART initiation two months after starting TB treatment. Routine data on the timing of ART initiation globally is limited, but surveys in some countries, such as India, suggest the feasibility of early ART initiation in TB patients, with 70% receiving ART within 30 days and 88% within 2 months. No significant differences in resource use are expected when comparing early and late ART initiation among TB patients, as all patients are anticipated to start ART within a few months. However, the increased incidence of IRIS with early ART initiation may require additional resources. Research gaps include the optimal timing of ART initiation in children living with HIV being treated for TB and patients with drug-resistant TB. Studies comparing ART initiation within 2 weeks and from 2 weeks to within 8 weeks of TB treatment are also needed, as well as research on the timing of ART initiation in adults and children with TB meningitis. Recent HIV infection, defined as the period up to 6 months following HIV acquisition, is characterized by the development of specific anti-HIV antibodies and the establishment of viral reservoirs. Early diagnosis during this phase offers an opportunity for treatment and prevention interventions with potentially significant public health impact. Initiating ART during recent HIV infection can reduce the size of latent viral reservoirs and delay viral rebound after ART discontinuation. Early diagnosis and treatment of individuals with very early HIV infection are critical for research on an HIV cure, as these individuals are likely to have smaller reservoirs, sustained immune function, and better immune restoration potential.
